why.correct: DNA content rises from 2 to 4 between 4 and 10 hours: that is S phase, when each DNA molecule is copied.
options: The only rise in the graph is from 2 to 4 units between 4 and 10 hours, which is DNA copying.
DNA content falls here, from 4 to 2: the cell divided at the end of meiosis I.
DNA content falls here, from 2 to 1: the cell divided at the end of meiosis II.
DNA content stays at 4 here: copying is finished and the cell is preparing for and starting meiosis I.

why.correct: At 2 hours the cell is in G1: 24 chromosomes, each one DNA molecule. At 24 hours meiosis I is over: homologs have separated, so the cell has 12 chromosomes, but each still has two sister chromatids. 12 × 2 = 24 DNA molecules either way, so the DNA content matches.
options: Meiosis I halves the number of chromosomes but leaves each one with two chromatids, so the DNA content equals that of a G1 cell.
This has the numbers reversed: the G1 cell is the diploid one, and meiosis I halves the chromosome count.
DNA content counts DNA molecules, not chromosomes. 24 single-chromatid chromosomes and 12 two-chromatid chromosomes hold the same amount.
Sister chromatids do not separate until meiosis II, so a cell between the two divisions still has two chromatids per chromosome; a G1 cell has one.

why.correct: At 16 hours the DNA has been copied (content 4) but the cell has not divided, so it still has 2n = 24 chromosomes, each made of 2 sister chromatids: 24 × 2 = 48.
The DNA was already copied by 10 hours. Without a spindle, chromosomes are not pulled to the poles, so neither division happens and the cell keeps its doubled DNA content of 4.
options: Copying finished before the drug was added, and the blocked cell does not divide, so it keeps 4 units.
Falling to 2 units needs the first division, which needs the spindle to pull homologs apart.
Falling to 1 unit needs both divisions; the drug blocks the spindle that drives each of them.
Reaching 8 units would need a second round of copying, which the question rules out.

why.correct: In meiosis II each of the 12 chromosomes splits into its two chromatids, one going to each new cell. Each new cell still has 12 chromosomes, but each is one DNA molecule, so the DNA halves. Because there was no S phase after meiosis I, nothing restores it.
options: Meiosis II splits sister chromatids; each new cell keeps 12 chromosomes, each now a single DNA molecule.
Homologs separated in meiosis I; after that the cell holds one chromosome of each kind, so there are no pairs left to separate.
DNA is not broken down; it is shared between the two new cells.
The graph shows no rise in DNA between the divisions, so no copying took place.

why.correct: Only in meiosis I do homologous chromosomes line up as side-by-side pairs, as in cell X.
options: Paired homologs lined up across the middle are the mark of metaphase I.
Six chromosomes lined up singly, two of each length, is metaphase of mitosis in a diploid cell.
Three chromosomes lined up singly, one of each length, is metaphase II in a haploid cell.
Single-chromatid chromosomes inside a nucleus: this cell has finished meiosis.

why.correct: A diploid cell in mitosis (W) has two of each kind. Y has one of each kind: it is haploid, which a cell becomes only after meiosis I has separated the homologs.
options: Being haploid, one of each kind, is the evidence that meiosis I has already happened.
W's chromosomes also have two sister chromatids, so this does not tell the two apart.
W's chromosomes are lined up the same way, so the arrangement alone does not tell them apart.
Chromosomes are not broken down in meiosis I; homologs are shared between the two new cells.

why.correct: Cell X has 6 chromosomes, each made of 2 sister chromatids: 6 × 2 = 12.
A haploid cell has one chromosome of each kind (n = 3 here), whatever the number of chromatids. Y and Z each have one long, one medium and one short chromosome.
options: W has two of each length: it is diploid (in mitosis).
X has two of each length, paired: it is diploid, in meiosis I, before the homologs separate.
Y has one chromosome of each length. Two chromatids per chromosome does not make it diploid.
Z has one chromosome of each length, each a single chromatid: a haploid cell at the end of meiosis.

why.correct: In meiosis II each of Y's three chromosomes splits into its two sister chromatids, one going to each pole. Each new cell gets one copy of each of the three: 3 chromosomes, each one chromatid.
options: Each pole gets one chromatid of every chromosome, so each new cell has 3 single-chromatid chromosomes.
The two chromatids of each chromosome separate in this division, so they no longer stay together.
Six chromatids are shared between two cells: three each, not six.
Meiosis II divides each chromosome's chromatids, not the set of chromosomes, so an odd number is no problem.

why.correct: Skin cells are diploid (2n = 78). Sperm are made by meiosis and are haploid: n = 78 ÷ 2 = 39.

Sister chromatids are made by copying one DNA molecule in S phase, so they are identical. The two chromosome 7s are homologs, one from each parent: same genes in the same order, but possibly different alleles.
options: Sister chromatids are copies; homologs come from different parents and may differ in alleles.
Homologs are not copies of each other: one came from the mother and one from the father.
Both sister chromatids were copied from the same chromosome, so they come from the same parent.
Homologs carry the same genes in the same order; what can differ is the version (allele) of each gene.

why.correct: Mitosis would give gametes the full 14 chromosomes. Fertilization adds the egg's and the sperm's chromosomes together: 14 + 14 = 28, double the parent's number.
options: Fertilization adds two gametes' chromosomes, so 14 + 14 = 28.
Mitosis keeps 14 in the gametes, but the offspring gets two gametes' worth.
Halving is what meiosis does; gametes made by mitosis would keep all 14.
Fertilization combines chromosomes; it never halves them.

why.correct: Fertilization joins a haploid sperm (n = 23) and a haploid egg (n = 23) into a diploid zygote (2n = 46).
options: A sperm and an egg, each with 23 chromosomes, join into a zygote with 46.
Meiosis I goes the other way: it turns a diploid cell into haploid cells.
Meiosis II starts and ends with haploid cells.
The zygote is already diploid; mitosis copies its set into new cells without changing the number.

why.correct: Meiosis halves the chromosome number by sending one homolog of each pair to each gamete, so the gamete keeps every kind of chromosome but only one copy of each.

variables.name: Number of chromosomes
variables.why: Meiosis halves the number: 23 in the sperm cell, 46 in the skin cell.

variables.name: Amount of DNA in the nucleus
variables.why: Half as many chromosomes, each a single chromatid, means half the DNA of a G1 skin cell.

variables.name: Number of different kinds of autosome (each kind counted once)
variables.why: Meiosis gives each gamete one of every pair, so the sperm cell still has all 22 kinds of autosome, just one copy of each.

variables.name: Number of copies of chromosome 1
variables.why: The skin cell has a homologous pair (two copies); the sperm cell received one of them.

why.correct: Copying (S phase) comes first; homologs then pair and line up as pairs, and separate in meiosis I. Meiosis II follows with no copying: chromosomes line up singly and sister chromatids separate.
Pairs of autosomes mean the cell is diploid, and X plus Y means it came from a male: a male body cell.
options: Diploid (pairs of every autosome) with XY: a male body cell.
A sperm cell is haploid: 22 single autosomes and either an X or a Y, not both.
Females have two X chromosomes and no Y.
An egg is haploid, with 22 single autosomes and one X.

why.correct: Meiosis II works like mitosis: chromosomes line up singly and their sister chromatids separate. What differs is that meiosis II happens in haploid cells with no S phase before it.
options: Both divisions end by separating sister chromatids.
In both, chromosomes line up one by one, not in pairs.
Homolog pairing happens in meiosis I, not in meiosis II or mitosis.
Mitosis follows an S phase, but meiosis II follows meiosis I with no copying in between.
Meiosis II starts with haploid cells, and mitosis keeps the number the same; meiosis I is the step that halves it.

why.correct: Meiosis I depends on each chromosome pairing with a matching homolog. Many horse and donkey chromosomes do not match, so they cannot pair properly and are not shared out one per gamete; the gametes get wrong sets and fail.
options: Meiosis needs matched homologous pairs, which a mix of horse and donkey chromosomes does not provide.
Copying works chromosome by chromosome; the total number does not matter, and the mule's body grows normally.
Body cells divide by mitosis; the mule grows normally, which shows mitosis works.
Mitosis separates sister chromatids, so any number of chromosomes, odd or even, is shared equally.

why.correct: A male bee has one set (n = 16). Dividing without halving keeps 16 in each sperm. The queen's eggs are made by meiosis (32 → 16). A fertilized egg gets 16 + 16 = 32, the female number.
options: Males are haploid, so gametes made without halving are still haploid, and 16 + 16 = 32.
The question says the male's division does not halve the number, and 24 is not the female number.
Nothing in the division doubles the chromosomes; the sperm keeps the male's 16.
Males come from unfertilized eggs; their 16 chromosomes came from the queen's egg, not from fertilization.

why.correct: Each tetrad is one homologous pair. 2n = 20 means 10 pairs, so 10 tetrads line up.
333 ÷ 8 = 41.6, about 42 times higher.
From 20 to 30 the rate climbs by 5 per 10,000 (6 to 11); from 35 to 45 it climbs by over 300 (26 to 333). The increase speeds up with age.
options: Small rises at first (6, 8, 11), then large ones (26, 91, 333).
The steps are 2, 3, 15, 65 and 242 per 10,000: far from equal.
6 to 8 and 8 to 11 are much less than doubling; 26 to 91 and 91 to 333 are more than tripling.
The rate already more than doubles between 30 and 35 (11 to 26), so it is not flat until 40.

why.correct: Paired homologs are held together until anaphase I. An egg released at 45 has been paused with its homologs paired for about 45 years, so there is more time for those links to fail and for a pair to separate wrongly in meiosis I, which fits both observations.
options: A long pause in prophase I gives more time for the pair's links to fail, explaining both the age effect and the meiosis I origin.
A copying error would not explain why the error appears in meiosis I separation, and copying happens only once before meiosis in eggs of any age.
The family studies show about 90% of extra chromosomes come from the egg, so a sperm explanation does not fit most cases.
An error after fertilization would not put the extra chromosome in the egg's meiosis I, which is where the DNA evidence places most cases.

why.correct: Nothing in the table measures fathers' ages, and the DNA studies place about 90% of extra chromosomes in eggs. The evidence supports a maternal-age effect, not a paternal one.
options: The grouping variable is the mother's age, and the DNA evidence points to eggs.
Continuous sperm production is a reason sperm might not carry long-paused errors; the data say nothing about fathers.
Partners' ages may be related, but the DNA studies show the extra copy usually comes from the egg.
Trisomy comes from chromosomes failing to separate (nondisjunction), not from crossing over.

why.correct: 22 pairs of autosomes would be 44; chromosome 21 has three copies instead of two, giving 45 autosomes, plus X and Y: 47.
Child A has one type from the father (1) and two from the mother (3 and 4). So the sperm carried one chromosome 21 (23 in all) and the egg carried two (24 in all).
options: Two of child A's three chromosome 21s match the mother's types, so the egg carried the extra one: 23 + 1 = 24.
Only one type from the father (1) is present, so the sperm carried a normal single chromosome 21.
An egg with 22 chromosomes would give 45 in the child, not 47.
An extra copy made after fertilization would duplicate one of the child's two types, not add the mother's second type.

why.correct: The egg carried types 3 and 4: one copy of each of the mother's two homologs. Homologs separate in meiosis I, so they ended up together because that division failed. An error in meiosis II would put two identical sister chromatids (3 and 3, or 4 and 4) in the egg.
options: Two different maternal types in one egg means the homologs did not separate: a meiosis I error.
Sister chromatids are identical near the centromere, so a meiosis II error gives two copies of one type, not 3 and 4.
One paternal type is the normal contribution of a sperm; the extra copy is maternal.
A mitosis error in the embryo would duplicate one of the child's existing copies and usually affect only some cells; it would not add the mother's second type.

why.correct: After a meiosis I error, one cell holds both homologs and the other holds none. Meiosis II then splits each into two gametes: two with two copies (n + 1) and two with none (n − 1).
options: A meiosis I error makes all four products abnormal: two n + 1 and two n − 1.
Normal gametes alongside an n + 1 gamete come from a meiosis II error, not meiosis I.
One n − 1 and two normal gametes, with one n + 1, is the meiosis II pattern.
The four products share four copies of chromosome 21 in total (two homologs, two chromatids each), so they cannot all carry two.

why.correct: Crossing over swaps pieces between homologs, so a type near the tip may have moved onto the other homolog. Near the centromere the type stays with its original homolog, so two different types in one gamete mean two homologs (meiosis I), two identical types mean two sister chromatids (meiosis II).
options: Without crossing over in that region, the type is a reliable label for each homolog.
The whole chromosome is copied in S phase, tips included.
Sister chromatids are identical copies; that sameness is what makes a meiosis II error show up as two copies of one type.
Whole chromosomes are passed on; recombinant chromosomes carry pieces of both homologs.

why.correct: 2n = 8 means n = 4 homologous pairs. Each pair can line up two ways, independently: 2⁴ = 16 combinations.
n = 3, so each parent makes 2³ = 8 kinds of gamete. Random fertilization pairs any of the 8 eggs with any of the 8 sperm: 8 × 8 = 64.
Only crossing over moves pieces between homologs, making a recombinant chromosome that carries some alleles from each.
options: Crossing over swaps matching pieces between a maternal and a paternal chromatid.
Independent assortment shuffles whole chromosomes; each chromosome stays maternal or paternal.
Fertilization combines two gametes' chromosomes but does not change any one chromosome.
Sister chromatids separate without exchanging anything.
Copying makes identical sister chromatids; it does not mix the homologs.

why.correct: Crossing over and independent assortment create variety only by mixing different alleles. If both homologs of every pair are the same, every gamete carries the same alleles, and so does every zygote.
options: With nothing different to shuffle, every gamete, and so every offspring, is the same.
Swapping matching pieces between identical homologs produces nothing new.
2ⁿ arrangements are possible, but if the homologs are identical every arrangement gives the same gamete.
Egg and pollen are each haploid; their fusion restores the diploid number, even from one parent.

why.correct: Crossing over happens in prophase I, while homologs are paired; they then line up independently at metaphase I; sister chromatids separate in meiosis II; fertilization comes last.
Removing crossing over removes recombinant chromosomes and so reduces variety, but it does not change the chromosome number or the shuffling of whole chromosomes by independent assortment.

variables.name: Number of chromosomes in each spore
variables.why: Separation is normal, so each spore still gets one chromosome of each kind.

variables.name: Number of different allele combinations among spores from many cells
variables.why: Without crossing over, alleles on one chromosome always travel together, so fewer combinations can arise.

variables.name: Fraction of spores with a chromosome carrying alleles from both homologs
variables.why: Such recombinant chromosomes are made only by crossing over, so they disappear.

variables.name: Number of whole-chromosome combinations possible from independent assortment
variables.why: Homologous pairs still line up independently at metaphase I, giving the same 2ⁿ combinations.

why.correct: X from the egg plus nothing from the sperm gives 45,X. A sperm with no sex chromosome results from nondisjunction of the X and Y in the father's meiosis I, or of sister chromatids in meiosis II.
options: 22 autosomes + X from the egg and 22 autosomes from the sperm give 45 chromosomes with one X.
This gives XXY, 47 chromosomes (Klinefelter syndrome).
This gives a typical XX girl with 46 chromosomes.
This gives 45,Y, which has no X; an embryo without any X does not survive.

why.correct: Down syndrome is usually trisomy 21: 47 chromosomes, with three copies of chromosome 21.
options: Trisomy 21, after a gamete with two chromosome 21s is fertilized.
Monosomy of an autosome such as 21 is almost never seen at birth; such embryos rarely survive.
A single X with no second sex chromosome is Turner syndrome.
Extra sex chromosomes cause other conditions, not Down syndrome.

why.correct: Normally each gamete gets 4. After meiosis I, one cell has 5 chromosomes (both homologs of the faulty pair) and the other 3. Meiosis II splits each normally: 5, 5, 3, 3.
options: Both cells after meiosis I are abnormal (5 and 3), and meiosis II passes that to all four gametes.
One n + 1, one n − 1 and two normal gametes is the result of an error in meiosis II.
Four normal gametes would mean no nondisjunction at all.
Chromosomes are not created: the four gametes share 16 in total (5 + 5 + 3 + 3), while 5, 5, 4, 4 adds up to 18.

why.correct: The sperm carried both an X and a Y. In a man, X and Y pair through their short matching region and separate in meiosis I; if they fail to separate, one sperm gets both. A meiosis II error would give XX or YY sperm, never XY.
options: X plus Y in one sperm means the X-Y pair stayed together: a meiosis I error.
A meiosis II error in the father gives a sperm with two identical X or two Y chromosomes, not X with Y.
Only one X came from the mother, so her egg was normal.
The mother contributed a single X, so her meiosis worked normally.

why.correct: Each of her 23 pairs sends one homolog or the other, independently. The second child matches the first for every pair with a chance of (1/2)²³ = 1 in 2²³, about 1 in 8.4 million.
options: Each of 23 independent pairs must match, each with a chance of 1/2: (1/2)²³ ≈ 1 in 8.4 million.
23 is the number of pairs; each pair is a separate 1-in-2 chance, and the chances multiply.
46 is the number of chromosomes; it is not the number of combinations.
1 in 2 is the chance of matching for one pair, not for all 23.

why.correct: The cuttings are genetically identical: if the parent lacks the rare combination, every plant dies. Seedlings each carry a new combination, so some may happen to have the one that survives.
options: Variety among seedlings raises the chance that some carry the surviving combination.
Identical plants share the same weakness; if one dies, they all do.
Meiosis and fertilization shuffle alleles that already exist; they do not invent alleles to order.
Plants of a species share genes but differ in alleles, and on farm 2 they differ in allele combinations.

why.correct: Unaffected parents (I-1 and I-2; II-3 and II-4) have affected children, so the allele is recessive. A daughter with an X-linked recessive trait needs an affected father, because he gives her his only X; III-1's father is unaffected, so the gene is on an autosome.
options: Affected children of unaffected parents point to recessive; an affected daughter of an unaffected father rules out X-linked recessive.
A dominant trait shows in anyone carrying the allele, so an affected child of two unaffected parents argues against dominant inheritance.
II-1 fits X-linked recessive, but III-1 does not: her father would have to be affected.
An affected son of an unaffected mother fits both autosomal and X-linked recessive, so it does not rule out X-linkage.

why.correct: Each unaffected parent of an affected child must carry one a allele: I-1 and I-2 (parents of II-1) and II-3 and II-4 (parents of III-1). II-2 and III-3 are unaffected children of two carriers and could be AA or Aa.
options: I-1 is unaffected but has an affected son, so he passed on an a allele: Aa.
I-2 is unaffected but has an affected son: Aa.
II-2 is unaffected (not aa), but he may have received A from both parents: AA or Aa.
II-3 is unaffected but has an affected daughter: Aa.
II-4 is unaffected but has an affected daughter, so despite no family history he carries a: Aa.
III-3 could be AA or Aa; nothing in the pedigree decides it.

why.correct: His parents are both Aa, so their children are AA, Aa, Aa or aa with equal chances. II-2 is unaffected, which removes aa and leaves three equally likely outcomes, two of them Aa: 2/3 ≈ 0.67.
Aa × Aa gives aa with probability 1/4. Being a boy has probability 1/2, independently. Product rule: 1/4 × 1/2 = 1/8 = 0.125.

III-3 is unaffected with Aa × Aa parents, so she is Aa with probability 2/3. The man is aa. If she is Aa, a child is aa with probability 1/2; if she is AA, never. Product rule: 2/3 × 1/2 = 1/3 ≈ 0.33.
The F1 kernels were heterozygous for both genes and showed purple and smooth, so those alleles are dominant.
options: A heterozygote shows the dominant phenotype: the F1 were purple and smooth.
Yellow and wrinkled disappeared in the F1 and returned in the F2: they are recessive.
Wrinkled was hidden in the heterozygous F1, so it is recessive.
Yellow was hidden in the heterozygous F1, so it is recessive.

why.correct: Purple: 216 + 79 = 295. Yellow: 70 + 25 = 95. 295 ÷ 95 = 3.1, close to the 3:1 of a monohybrid cross.
Yellow and wrinkled is the double recessive class, 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16 of the F2. 390 ÷ 16 = 24.4, about 24 kernels (25 were counted).

Each F1 is PpSs. Segregation gives each gamete one allele of each gene, and because the two pairs assort independently, the four combinations are equally likely (1/4 each). Random fertilization of 4 × 4 gamete types gives 16 equally likely boxes: 9 P_S_, 3 P_ss, 3 ppS_, 1 ppss.
options: Independent assortment makes four equal gamete types; 4 × 4 random combinations give 9:3:3:1.
The ratio comes from independent assortment of separate chromosome pairs; crossing over affects genes on the same chromosome.
Dominance decides what the offspring look like, not which alleles enter gametes; each allele goes into half the gametes.
Only two gamete types would give a 3:1 pattern of purple smooth to yellow wrinkled, with no purple wrinkled or yellow smooth kernels.

why.correct: A testcross to ppss means every offspring gets p and s from that parent, so the offspring show directly which alleles the tested plant's gametes carried. PpSs makes PS, Ps, pS and ps equally, giving a 1:1:1:1 ratio.
options: In a testcross the offspring phenotypes mirror the tested plant's gametes: four equal classes mean PpSs.
Another purple, smooth parent can hide recessive alleles, so the result would not reveal the genotype.
Offspring that are purple and smooth every time would mean the plant is PPSS, not PpSs.
Selfing PpSs gives four phenotypes in a 9:3:3:1 ratio, not 3:1.

why.correct: For each gene, Aa × Aa gives aa with probability 1/4. Product rule: 1/4 × 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/64, so 1 in 64.
Aa × Aa: dominant phenotype (AA or Aa) with probability 3/4. Bb × bb: Bb with probability 1/2. Product rule: 3/4 × 1/2 = 3/8 = 0.375.
Ff × Ff gives FF, Ff, Ff and ff, each 1/4. Only FF is neither affected nor a carrier: 1/4.
options: FF is one of four equally likely outcomes.
1/2 is the chance of being a carrier (Ff).
3/4 is the chance of being unaffected (FF or Ff), which includes carriers.
2/3 is the chance that an unaffected child is a carrier, a different question.

why.correct: White offspring are bb, so each got a b from the black parent as well as from the white one. The black parent is Bb, and Bb × bb predicts a 1:1 ratio, close to 7:6.
options: White offspring prove the black parent carries b; a 1:1 ratio fits Bb × bb.
A BB parent would give only Bb offspring, all black.
A bb guinea pig would be white, not black.
This testcross does decide it: one white offspring is enough to show the black parent carries b.

why.correct: Her father gave her his X with the allele, so she is X<sup>B</sup>X<sup>b</sup>. The man is X<sup>b</sup>Y. Sons get Y from him and either X from her: 1/2 X<sup>b</sup>Y. Daughters get his X<sup>b</sup> and either of hers: 1/2 X<sup>b</sup>X<sup>b</sup>.
options: Mother X<sup>B</sup>X<sup>b</sup> × father X<sup>b</sup>Y gives color-blind sons and daughters, half of each.
Every daughter receives the father's X<sup>b</sup>, so a daughter is color-blind whenever her mother also passes X<sup>b</sup> (half the time).
Sons get their X from the mother, who passes X<sup>b</sup> half the time.
One quarter is the result for a carrier mother and an unaffected father, not a color-blind father.

why.correct: Males are hemizygous for X-linked genes: there is no second copy on the Y to mask a recessive allele. A female shows the trait only if both her X chromosomes carry it, which is much rarer.
options: With one X and no matching gene on the Y, one recessive allele is enough in a male.
The Y lacks most X genes; it does not carry a matching allele for this gene.
A son gets his X from his mother and his Y from his father.
DNA is copied once before meiosis in both sexes; copying does not depend on the allele.

why.correct: His unaffected mother was hh, so he is Hh. His daughter's mother is unaffected (hh), so the daughter got H with probability 1/2. At 20, before the usual age of onset, having no symptoms tells us almost nothing.
options: Hh × hh gives Hh in half of the children, and her age means symptoms would not be expected yet.
1/4 would need two heterozygous parents and asks for hh; here one parent is Hh and the other hh.
With an allele whose effects begin in adulthood, a 20-year-old can carry it without symptoms.
Her father is heterozygous, so he passes H to half his children, not to every child.

why.correct: The two alleles of a gene sit on the two homologs. When the homologs go to opposite poles in meiosis I, the alleles go to different cells, which is segregation.
options: Separating homologs separates the two alleles a diploid cell carries.
Sister chromatids carry identical alleles, and each gamete ends with one chromatid, so one allele.
Crossing over makes new combinations of alleles of different genes; segregation is about the two alleles of one gene.
Copying makes identical sister chromatids; it does not separate the two different alleles.

why.correct: Independent assortment follows from separate homologous pairs lining up independently at metaphase I. Dominance, the traits involved and the way the parents were bred do not affect it.
options: Separate chromosome pairs line up independently, so their alleles sort independently.
Dominance affects how a genotype looks, not how alleles are sorted into gametes.
What the genes do does not matter; where they are on the chromosomes does.
True-breeding parents give a uniform F1, but the sorting happens in the F1's meiosis.
Selfing and crossing F1 plants give the same F2 when the F1 all have the same genotype.

why.correct: Complex shared mechanisms are most simply explained by descent from a common ancestor that already had them.
options: Shared, detailed machinery is evidence of common ancestry.
Several independent origins of the same detailed system is far less likely than one shared origin.
Shared features point to a shared ancestor, not to one living group being the ancestor of the others.
Inheritance is not learned; it works through chromosomes in every generation.

why.correct: True-breeding parents are needed first; their cross gives a uniform F1; selfing the F1 gives the F2, whose counts show the 3:1 ratio.
For an X-linked gene, which parent carries the allele matters, because sons get their only X from their mother. Swapping the parents' phenotypes changes the sons' results but not the daughters'.

variables.name: Fraction of sons with white eyes
variables.why: Sons get their X from the mother. In cross 2 she has only X<sup>w</sup>, so every son is white-eyed; in cross 1 none are.

variables.name: Fraction of daughters with white eyes
variables.why: In both crosses each daughter gets one red allele (from the father in cross 2, the mother in cross 1), so no daughters are white-eyed.

variables.name: Fraction of daughters who carry the white allele
variables.why: In both crosses every daughter gets exactly one X<sup>w</sup>: from the father in cross 1, from the mother in cross 2.

variables.name: Fraction of all offspring with red eyes
variables.why: Cross 1 gives red eyes in every fly; cross 2 gives red-eyed daughters and white-eyed sons, so only half.

why.correct: The F1 female got B P from one parent and b p from the other. Offspring showing B with p, or b with P, carry combinations neither of her parents had: recombinants.
options: Gray-purple and black-red mix the grandparents' combinations, and they are the two small classes.
These match the original true-breeding parents' combinations: parental types.
These share a body color; one class is parental, the other recombinant.
These share a body color; one class is parental, the other recombinant.

why.correct: Recombinants: 31 + 33 = 64. 64 ÷ 1,000 × 100 = 6.4%, so the genes are about 6.4 map units apart.
Independent assortment predicts a 1:1:1:1 testcross ratio: 1,000 ÷ 4 = 250 flies per class.
Four classes give df = 4 − 1 = 3, critical value 7.82 at p = 0.05. 760 is far larger, so the deviation from 1:1:1:1 is very unlikely to be chance. Too many parental types fits linkage.
options: df = 3, and 760 > 7.82: reject; excess parental types point to linkage.
Degrees of freedom are the number of classes minus one: 4 − 1 = 3, not 4.
A χ² larger than the critical value means reject, not fail to reject.
Rejecting independent assortment points the other way: the genes are close on the same chromosome.

why.correct: A crossover is a reciprocal exchange: when a B P chromatid and a b p chromatid swap their p/P ends, the result is one B p and one b P. So the two recombinant types are made in equal numbers, as are the two parental types.
options: Reciprocal exchange makes the two recombinant types in pairs, so they come out about equal.
Equal survival does not explain why the parental classes are about 15 times larger than the recombinant classes.
The male is bbpp, so every sperm carries b p; the variety comes from the female's eggs.
Recombinants are only 6.4% here; crossovers between these two close genes are rare.

why.correct: ee dogs cannot put pigment into hair, so they are yellow whether they make black (B_) or brown (bb) pigment: BBee, Bbee and bbee are yellow.
options: ee blocks pigment in the hair, so the B gene's alleles do not show.
BBee and Bbee are also yellow; ee alone is enough.
bb with E_ is chocolate, not yellow: brown pigment is made and deposited.
E is dominant: one copy lets pigment into the hair.

why.correct: Three classes give df = 3 − 1 = 2, critical value 5.99. 0.10 is far below it, so the small deviations are consistent with chance: fail to reject 9:3:4.
options: df = 2 and 0.10 < 5.99: the data fit the hypothesis.
There are three color classes, so df = 2, not 3.
A χ² below the critical value means fail to reject, not reject.
A test can fail to reject a hypothesis but never proves it true.

why.correct: Every puppy gets B and e from the yellow parent and b and E from the chocolate parent: BbEe. B makes black pigment and E lets it into the hair, so the puppies are black, a color neither parent shows.
options: BbEe: the B allele means black pigment is made, and the E allele lets it into the hair.
Puppies get one E from the chocolate parent, so they can deposit pigment.
Puppies get one B from the yellow parent, and B (black) is dominant to b.
Each parent is homozygous at both genes, so every puppy has the same genotype, BbEe.

why.correct: This is epistasis: ee masks the B gene. The 16 combinations still form 9:3:3:1 by genotype class (B_E_, B_ee, bbE_, bbee), but B_ee and bbee look the same, giving 9 black : 3 chocolate : 4 yellow.
options: Epistasis makes two genotype classes share one phenotype: 3 + 1 = 4 yellow.
The genes are on different chromosomes; linkage would change the class sizes, not merge two classes.
A lethal class would leave 15 parts, not 16; the yellow count fits 4/16 of all puppies.
Black and chocolate are distinct classes here, with 92 and 29 puppies; nothing blends.

why.correct: Eggs from a green branch give green seedlings whatever the pollen; eggs from a white branch give white seedlings; eggs from a variegated branch give a mix. The pollen source makes no difference.
options: The seedlings' color follows the egg-giving branch in every row.
Pollen from variegated or white branches still gives green seedlings when the eggs come from a green branch.
Eggs from a white branch fertilized by green pollen give white seedlings, so green does not appear in every cross.
No cross gives a 3:1 ratio; the result depends on the egg's branch.

why.correct: Chloroplasts carry their own DNA and are passed on in the cytoplasm. An egg brings plenty of cytoplasm; the pollen's sperm brings almost none. So the seedling inherits the chloroplasts of the egg's branch: green, white or a mix.
options: Chloroplasts travel with the egg's cytoplasm, so seedlings match the egg-giving branch.
A nuclear allele would give the same result whichever plant gave the eggs, and these crosses differ by direction.
Four o'clocks have no sex chromosomes; each flower makes both eggs and pollen.
The nucleus does not destroy chloroplasts; the sperm cell brings little or no chloroplast DNA to begin with.

why.correct: Egg and sperm each carry one set of nuclear chromosomes, so for an autosomal gene it does not matter which parent is the mother. A difference between reciprocal crosses points to a sex chromosome (which this plant lacks) or to the cytoplasm.
options: Nuclear alleles come equally from both parents, so reciprocal crosses agree.
Swapping parents does not change the result for a nuclear gene on a non-sex chromosome.
Eggs and sperm both carry a full haploid set of nuclear chromosomes.
9:3:3:1 needs two genes and double heterozygotes; it does not describe these crosses.

why.correct: Like chloroplasts in plants, mitochondria are passed on in the egg's cytoplasm. Children get their mother's mitochondria, so an affected mother can pass the condition to sons and daughters, and an affected father, as a rule, cannot.
options: Mitochondria come from the egg, so the mother's mitochondrial DNA is the one inherited.
The father's mitochondria are not passed on in the sperm, as a rule.
A 1:1 pattern is for nuclear genes; mitochondrial genes follow the mother.
Mitochondrial DNA is not on the X; an affected mother can pass it to children of either sex.

why.correct: C<sup>R</sup>C<sup>W</sup> × C<sup>R</sup>C<sup>W</sup> gives 1 C<sup>R</sup>C<sup>R</sup> : 2 C<sup>R</sup>C<sup>W</sup> : 1 C<sup>W</sup>C<sup>W</sup>. With incomplete dominance each genotype has its own color, so the phenotype ratio equals the genotype ratio.
options: Each genotype looks different, so 1:2:1 genotypes give 1:2:1 colors.
Pink is the heterozygote, so it cannot breed true or be a dominant class.
3:1 would need red to be dominant, but the heterozygote is pink, not red.
Pink plants are heterozygous, so they produce pink offspring as well as red and white.

why.correct: A type O child is ii and got an i from each parent. A type AB man is I<sup>A</sup>I<sup>B</sup> and has no i to give, so he cannot be the father. Men with type A, B or O can all carry i.
options: I<sup>A</sup>I<sup>B</sup> carries no i allele, so he cannot give the child one.
A type A man can be I<sup>A</sup>i and pass i.
A type B man can be I<sup>B</sup>i and pass i.
A type O man is ii and passes i to every child.

why.correct: The child needs I<sup>A</sup> from the father (½) and I<sup>B</sup> from the mother (½): ½ × ½ = ¼ = 0.25. Each of A, B, AB and O is ¼ in this cross.
Both alleles show their full effect side by side: some hairs red, some white. That is codominance. Incomplete dominance would give one in-between color in every hair, such as pink.
options: Both colors appear unchanged in the same animal: codominance.
A blend would make each hair an in-between color; here each hair is fully red or fully white.
With complete dominance the calf would be one color, like a homozygous parent.
One gene with two alleles is enough to explain this; no second gene is masking another.

why.correct: An offspring can have 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6 capital-letter alleles, and height depends only on that number: 7 classes. With more genes the classes multiply and the distribution looks continuous, as for polygenic traits such as human height.
One gene affects several different traits because its protein works in several tissues: pleiotropy.
options: One gene with many effects is the definition of pleiotropy.
Epistasis is one gene masking another gene; here a single gene acts in many places.
Polygenic inheritance is many genes affecting one trait, the reverse situation.
Codominance describes how two alleles show in a heterozygote; carriers here are unaffected.

why.correct: The largest distance (A–B, 12) spans the two outer genes, so C lies between them. A–C (8) + C–B (4) = 12 = A–B, which fits A – C – B.
options: A–B is the longest distance, so the A gene and the B gene are at the ends and C is in the middle: 8 + 4 = 12.
B in the middle would need A–B + B–C = A–C, but 12 + 4 is not 8.
A in the middle would need B–A + A–C = B–C, but 12 + 8 is not 4.
This puts A in the middle (C–A 8, A–B 12), which would make C–B 20, not 4.

why.correct: Independent assortment predicts four equal classes in a testcross. Two large (parental) and two small (recombinant) classes show the alleles travel together on one chromosome.
options: A big excess of two classes is the signature of linkage: parental combinations kept together.
Equal classes are what independent assortment predicts, so they are evidence against linkage.
Each gene alone gives 1:1 in a testcross whether or not the genes are linked.
Three quarters dominant for both is not expected in a testcross of AaBb, linked or not.
In a testcross Aa × aa gives half aa offspring, so this result would mean the parent was AA.

why.correct: Recombination frequency rises with the distance between linked genes, so the farther pair gives more recombinants and fewer parental types; the classes and the chromosome number stay the same.

variables.name: Recombination frequency
variables.why: More distance between the genes gives more room for a crossover between them, so more recombinant gametes: about 30% instead of 5%.

variables.name: Percentage of parental-type offspring
variables.why: Parental and recombinant offspring add to 100%; more recombinants means fewer parental types (about 70% instead of 95%).

variables.name: Number of phenotype classes among the offspring
variables.why: Both testcrosses give the same four classes (two parental, two recombinant); only their sizes differ.

variables.name: Number of chromosomes in each gamete
variables.why: Crossing over swaps pieces between homologs; it does not change how many chromosomes a gamete gets.

why.correct: From pH 4.5 to 7.0, blue plants go from 8 to 0 and pink plants from 0 to 8, while aluminum falls from 210 to 15 µg/g.
options: Blue at low pH, pink at high pH, and aluminum drops as pH rises.
This reverses the trend: blue flowers are at the acidic, low-pH end, where aluminum is highest.
Aluminum falls more than tenfold across the range, so it does not stay the same.
Color changes clearly, from 8 blue plants at pH 4.5 to 8 pink plants at pH 7.0.

why.correct: Cuttings are clones: genetically identical. Seedlings come from sexual reproduction and differ in their alleles, so a color difference between seedling groups could be genetic. Holding genotype constant isolates the environmental variable, soil pH.
options: Identical genotypes mean any difference between groups comes from the environment.
Speed may be convenient, but it is not the reason that matters for the conclusion.
Hydrangea seedlings can flower; the issue is that each seedling has a different genotype.
Nothing suggests cuttings and seedlings differ in aluminum uptake; the key point is a shared genotype.

why.correct: In the table, pH and aluminum change together, so either could cause the color. Holding pH constant and changing only aluminum separates them: if the low-aluminum plants turn pink in acidic soil, aluminum is the cause.
options: This changes aluminum while holding pH fixed, so it separates the two possible causes.
More measurements across the same pH values would still have aluminum and pH changing together.
Seedlings add genetic differences and still change pH and aluminum together.
Checking pH improves the existing data but does not separate aluminum from acidity.

why.correct: Blue or purple at pH 6.0: 1 + 4 = 5 of 8 plants. 5 ÷ 8 × 100 = 62.5%.
pH 5.5: 105 to 135 µg/g; pH 6.0: 48 to 72 µg/g. The intervals do not overlap, so the difference is likely real.
options: 105-135 and 48-72 do not overlap.
190-230 and 162-198 overlap, so this difference is not shown to be real.
17-33 and 9-21 overlap, so this difference is not shown to be real.
The pH 5.5 and 6.0 intervals are well separated.

why.correct: At 29 °C the mean is 52% female, the closest point to 50%. This is the pivotal temperature for this species.
Reading the graph: 18% female at 28 °C, 86% at 30 °C. A 2 °C rise near the pivotal temperature shifts the sex ratio strongly toward females.
options: 28 °C gives about 18% females and 30 °C about 86%: a large shift toward females.
This reverses the direction: warmer eggs give more females in this species.
In this species sex is set by temperature, so the ratio changes with warming.
At 30 °C the mean is 86% female, not 100%; some males still hatch.

why.correct: If each nest went to one incubator, a nest whose eggs were, for genetic reasons, more likely to become female would be confused with the effect of its temperature. Splitting every nest across all temperatures controls for that.
options: Spreading each nest's eggs across every temperature stops nest differences from being mistaken for temperature effects.
Equal numbers help, but the purpose of splitting nests is to control for differences between nests.
Sex is expected to differ with temperature, even among eggs from one mother.
Sex cannot identify a nest; the nests' eggs would be labeled directly.

why.correct: At 31 °C the interval is 94% to 100%, which includes the 100% seen at 32 °C. The difference is not shown to be real.
options: The 31 °C interval reaches 100%, so it overlaps the 32 °C value.
Means can differ by chance; overlapping ± 2 SE intervals mean the difference is not shown to be real.
A zero-width bar at 32 °C does not stop it overlapping the 31 °C interval.
Means of percentages from several nests can be compared with ± 2 SE intervals like any other mean.

why.correct: The rabbit's enzyme for dark pigment is active only at cooler temperatures. Cooled skin lets it work, so the regrowing hair is dark, as on the ears and paws.
options: Cold lets the temperature-sensitive enzyme work, so dark pigment is made.
Every cell has the same genotype; the back is white only because it is warm.
The fur regrows; its color depends on the skin temperature while it grows.
Temperature changes how the enzyme works, not the alleles in the DNA.

why.correct: Their allele codes for a temperature-sensitive enzyme: like a protein above its optimum, it is denatured at core body temperature, but holds its shape in cooler skin, where dark pigment is made.
options: A temperature-sensitive enzyme explains why only cool parts are dark.
Body cells share one genotype; the difference is temperature.
Pigment is made in the hair-growing cells of each patch of skin, not moved there.
Kittens are born pale and darken as their extremities cool, which fits temperature, not a second gene.

why.correct: Diet cannot change alleles. It changes the environment her enzyme-less cells work in: little phenylalanine, so none builds up to harm the brain. Same genotype, different phenotype.
options: Genotype pp is unchanged; the environment (diet) changes the outcome.
Food does not change DNA; she is still pp.
She has the genotype for PKU; the diet prevents its effects.
She will pass a p allele to every child, as she carries no P.

why.correct: The diet changes the environment, and so the phenotype, but not the genotype or what is passed to the next generation.

variables.name: Phenylalanine level in the blood
variables.why: Less phenylalanine is eaten, so less builds up when the enzyme to break it down is missing.

variables.name: Number of copies of the PKU allele in each cell
variables.why: Diet does not change alleles: both children are pp.

variables.name: Risk of harm to brain development
variables.why: The harm comes from phenylalanine building up; keeping it low prevents it.

variables.name: Chance of passing a PKU allele to each future child
variables.why: Each child is pp and passes p in every gamete, whatever the diet.

why.correct: With identical genotypes, the 8 cm difference must come from the environment, here nutrition. Height is polygenic and multifactorial.
options: Same genes, different heights: the environment acts within a genetic range.
Identical twins have the same alleles; neither received a different one.
Genes still matter: heights of identical twins are much more alike than those of unrelated people.
Identical twins come from one zygote, so their genotypes match.

why.correct: Plotting height against nitrogen gives a line for each genotype (a norm of reaction). The lines cross, so neither genotype is taller everywhere: the effect of genotype depends on the environment, an interaction of genes and environment.
options: Crossing norms of reaction mean the ranking of genotypes changes with the environment.
Variety 2 is taller in rich soil, so neither variety is taller in both environments.
Soil nitrogen changes growth, not DNA; each clone keeps its own genotype.
Genotype clearly matters, since the two varieties respond differently to the same soils.

why.correct: Plasticity is one genotype giving different phenotypes in different environments: the same arrowhead plant makes two leaf shapes, and the same water flea grows spines when predators are around.
options: The same plant, so the same genotype, makes different leaves under water and in air.
The same genotype grows different spines depending on a chemical cue in its environment.
This shows how alleles are inherited (incomplete dominance), not the environment changing a genotype's phenotype.
This is inheritance of chloroplasts through the egg, not an environmental effect.
This shows independent assortment of alleles, not an environmental effect.

why.correct: Acidity dissolves aluminum; dissolved aluminum can be taken up by the roots and carried to the flowers, where it binds the pigment and changes its color to blue.
A common-garden experiment puts both kinds in one environment. If the difference remains, it cannot be caused by their different home environments, so genes must contribute.
options: In the same environment, a remaining difference must come from genotype.
Measuring more plants in their own habitats still mixes genes with environment.
Staying short at home is what both a genetic and an environmental explanation predict.
A soil difference suggests an environmental cause; it does not test for a genetic one.

why.correct: Soil pH changes how the pigment looks, not the DNA. The seedlings carry the same kinds of alleles; in acidic soil they take up aluminum and bloom blue.
options: The environment of the seedlings, acidic soil, sets their color, as it did for the parent.
The parent's pink color was an environmental effect that is not passed on in its alleles.
Dominance is a property of alleles in a heterozygote; liming soil does not change it.
Changing the soil pH does not damage DNA.
